questions.stem:
Argument: 'Students who study in the morning perform better academically.'
Which of the following WEAKENS this argument?

options.option_text: Studies show morning students have lower stress levels
A recent study found that academic performance depends primarily on total hours studied, not time of day
Many universities schedule important exams in the morning
Morning students tend to sleep earlier

questions.explanation: B is correct. To WEAKEN an argument, find a fact that undermines the causal link. The argument claims morning study → better performance. If performance depends on total hours, not time of day, then the time-of-day factor is not the cause — this directly weakens the argument.

questions.stem:
Conclusion: 'All politicians are corrupt.'
Which statement, if true, SUPPORTS this conclusion?

options.option_text: Many politicians have been found guilty of financial misconduct
Every politician investigated in the past decade was found to have engaged in corrupt practices
Some politicians have clean records
The political system lacks transparency

questions.explanation: B is correct. The conclusion is 'ALL politicians are corrupt.' The supporting statement must be consistent with ALL being corrupt. Option B (every politician investigated = corrupt) most strongly supports this — though note that 'investigated' ≠ 'all politicians.' Of the options, B is the strongest support for the blanket conclusion.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Exercise reduces the risk of heart disease by 30%.'
Which is the STRONGEST assumption behind this statement?

options.option_text: All people who exercise will avoid heart disease
The 30% figure was derived from credible research on a sufficient sample size
People who don't exercise will definitely get heart disease
Heart disease is the only disease affected by exercise

questions.explanation: B is correct. An ASSUMPTION is an unstated premise that must be true for the statement to hold. For the 30% claim to be valid, it must be based on credible research — if the research is flawed, the claim collapses. This is the core assumption behind any statistical claim.

questions.stem:
'Since fewer people bought cars this quarter, the economy must be slowing down.'
What is the FLAW in this reasoning?

options.option_text: Car sales are the most important economic indicator
The conclusion assumes that fewer car sales is the ONLY possible explanation for a slowing economy
Fewer car sales could be due to other reasons (e.g., fuel prices, new car tech launches delayed) unrelated to the overall economy
The economy always reflects car sales trends

questions.explanation: C is correct. The reasoning jumps from fewer car sales to a slowing economy without considering other causes. The FLAW = false causation / hasty generalisation. Fewer car sales might be due to supply chain issues, high prices, or consumer preference shifts — not necessarily economic slowdown. This is the classic 'correlation ≠ causation' error.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Most successful entrepreneurs dropped out of school.'
Can we conclude: 'Dropping out of school leads to success as an entrepreneur'?

options.option_text: Yes — the evidence clearly shows dropping out causes entrepreneurial success
No — the statement describes a pattern among successful entrepreneurs but doesn't prove dropping out CAUSES success
Yes — if most successful ones dropped out, then dropping out is the key factor
Not enough information to decide

questions.explanation: B is correct. Classic SURVIVOR BIAS and CORRELATION vs CAUSATION error. The statement observes a pattern among successful entrepreneurs but ignores: (1) most dropouts are NOT successful; (2) correlation doesn't prove causation. The conclusion that 'dropping out CAUSES success' is logically unwarranted.

questions.stem: Which LOGICAL FALLACY is committed: 'You can't trust Dr. Sharma's opinion on climate change because he drives a petrol car.'

options.option_text: False dilemma
Ad hominem
Straw man
Circular reasoning

questions.explanation: B is correct. AD HOMINEM fallacy = attacking the person instead of their argument. 'He drives a petrol car' is irrelevant to whether his climate change opinion is scientifically valid. Attacking personal behaviour to dismiss an argument is a classic ad hominem.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a STRONG argument for increasing the minimum wage?

options.option_text: Other countries have higher minimum wages
Increasing minimum wage will give workers more buying power, stimulating economic growth
Workers deserve to be paid more for their efforts
Minimum wage hasn't been increased in years

questions.explanation: B is correct. A STRONG argument has: (1) a clear logical mechanism, (2) evidence or economic rationale, (3) relevance to the conclusion. B provides a clear economic mechanism (increased purchasing power → demand → growth). The other options rely on emotional appeals, comparisons, or non-logical bases.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Reading improves vocabulary. Riya has an excellent vocabulary.'
Conclusion: 'Riya reads a lot.'
Is this conclusion valid?

options.option_text: Yes — reading improves vocabulary, so excellent vocabulary must come from reading
No — the conclusion commits the fallacy of affirming the consequent
Yes — the relationship is bidirectional
Cannot be determined at all

questions.explanation: B is correct. FALLACY OF AFFIRMING THE CONSEQUENT: If P then Q; Q is true; therefore P is true — INVALID. Reading (P) → good vocabulary (Q). Riya has good vocabulary (Q). Therefore Riya reads (P) = INVALID. Riya's vocabulary could come from other sources (conversations, word games, formal education).

questions.stem: Which is a WEAK argument against banning tobacco products?

options.option_text: Tobacco farming supports millions of livelihoods
My grandfather smoked for 70 years and lived to 90
Banning tobacco would create a black market, potentially worse outcomes
Adults have the right to make their own decisions about legal substances

questions.explanation: B is correct. WEAK ARGUMENT. 'My grandfather smoked and lived to 90' is ANECDOTAL EVIDENCE — using a single personal example to counter population-level statistical evidence. One exception doesn't disprove the general rule. This is the 'hasty generalisation from a single case' fallacy.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'The population of City X has grown by 20% in 5 years.'
Conclusion: 'City X is becoming more prosperous.'
Is this inference valid?

options.option_text: Yes — population growth always indicates prosperity
No — population growth can occur for reasons other than prosperity
Yes — growing cities are always prosperous
The statement provides no information for any inference

questions.explanation: B is correct. Population growth does NOT necessarily indicate prosperity. Alternative explanations: high birth rate, migration from disaster areas, refugee influx, etc. The inference 'population growth → prosperity' is INVALID without additional data on economic indicators. This tests the ability to identify unwarranted inferences.
